direction: Keep the D003 evaluation design and reframe the contribution as implementation-and-measurement rather than problem identification: enforce valid-time membership at retrieval time (post hoc, across BM25/dense/hybrid), and measure clause-level point-in-time recovery and version contamination, with answer accuracy co-primary only on answer-differential queries. Present the benchmark as filling the named clause-granularity gap, not as discovering it, and present valid-time gating as the correct signal to enforce at retrieval time rather than as a new concept.
hypothesis: Enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership at retrieval time, rather than only encoding time in representations, reduces clause-level point-in-time retrieval failures (returning text not in force at the query date) relative to semantic-only retrieval and to elapsed-time decay, and the reduction is larger where successive clause versions are near-duplicates and the authoritative version is not the latest.
rationale: The legal-retrieval review states that diachronic failure is the least well integrated into mainstream practice, that solutions are stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement, and that document-granularity versioning obscures structural-unit differentials. This confirms the gap is real and explicitly recognized, while also confirming that the signal (valid-time/bitemporal) and the framing (architecture-agnostic) are not novel. The direction therefore narrows to what remains measurable and unmeasured: retrieval-time enforcement across retrievers plus clause-level point-in-time recovery metrics. It deserves investigation next because it is the smallest claim not contradicted by the retrieved evidence, it is falsifiable with existing tools, and a negative result (retrieval-time gating adds little) would itself be informative about where temporal handling belongs.
research_question: Does enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership at retrieval time, post hoc across sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers, improve clause-level point-in-time retrieval (returning the text in force at the query date and avoiding superseded or not-yet-in-force versions), compared with semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, and representation-level temporal handling?
